How GPT-5.6 Sol helps run quantum computing experiments

📅 08 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecting GPT‑5.6 Sol to laboratory software to run and refine routine measurements on quantum chips freed Beatriz Yankelevich to focus on experiment design and data analysis.
  • In a recent development, quantum computing is an emerging technology that uses the unique properties of quantum mechanics to process information.
  • Beatriz Yankelevich, a graduate student in MIT’s Engineering Quantum Systems Group (EQuS), used GPT‑5.6 Sol, harnessed to Codex, to explore whether AI could streamline her experimental workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecting GPT‑5.6 Sol to laboratory software to run and refine routine measurements on quantum chips freed Beatriz Yankelevich to focus on experiment design and data analysis.

In a recent development, quantum computing is an emerging technology that uses the unique properties of quantum mechanics to process information. It could one day better simulate complex materials and molecules. Unlike conventional processors, quantum processors are built with quantum bits, or qubits. Preparing and running qubit experiments can take months and require hundreds to thousands of preliminary measurements—work that AI is poised to help with.

Beatriz Yankelevich, a graduate student in MIT’s Engineering Quantum Systems Group (EQuS), used GPT‑5.6 Sol, harnessed to Codex, to explore whether AI could streamline her experimental workflow. The MIT group studies superconducting qubits, which are cooled to near absolute zero inside specialized devices called dilution refrigerators. These qubits perform operations quickly, are precisely controlled using microwave signals, and can be made using familiar manufacturing techniques and arranged on a chip.

Once a superconducting qubit chip has been fabricated, packaged, and cooled, researchers interact with it entirely through software, making Yankelevich’s experiments a natural testbed for AI agents. Connecting Codex to the lab software that coordinates experiments allowed it to run measurements, analyze the results, and decide what to try next. Yankelevich found that GPT‑5.6 Sol could often complete routine measurement workflows autonomously, saving her significant amounts of time and allowing experiments to run without constant supervision. This freed her to spend more time on analyzing results, designing experiments, and planning out the next steps in her research.

A packaged qubit chip (left) sits inside an open dilution refrigerator (right). CREDIT: EQuS group.

Sources indicate that superconducting qubits are often called artificial atoms because, like atoms, they can only occupy specific energy levels. Microwave pulses move qubits between these levels and probe their quantum state. Researchers design and calibrate the pulse sequences sent to the chip, then digitize and analyse the returning signals. These measurements reveal each qubit’s resonance frequencies, which allows researchers to accurately control the qubit; how long the qubit retains quantum information; and the settings needed to perform computations.

It has been revealed that calibrating qubits requires a series of interdependent measurements, with each result shaping what happens next. Qubit properties can occasionally drift, and unexpected physical behavior can cause inconsistent results. Experienced researchers can recognize these changes and adapt when they occur. This combination of software control, repeated measurements, and adaptive decision-making also makes qubit calibration a compelling use case for AI agents.

Yankelevich tested GPT‑5.6 Sol’s ability to run measurements on an uncalibrated six-qubit chip, one of a standard type that EQuS routinely uses to benchmark its fabrication process. She provided Codex with measurement-specific skills explaining how to run and evaluate each experiment. Using these skills and the chip’s design targets, GPT‑5.6 Sol chose measurement parameters, operated the hardware, analyzed the resulting data, and then either refined the measurement or saved the result for use in the next measurement.

When the signals were clear, Codex completed a standard sequence of measurements with little researcher intervention. It identified the qubit’s transition frequencies, calibrated the pulses used to control and read it, and determined how long the qubit retained quantum information.

In a recent development, A set of calibration measurements for one qubit, completed autonomously by GPT‑5.6 Sol. CREDIT: EQuS group.

It has been revealed that A set of calibration measurements for one qubit, completed autonomously by GPT‑5.6 Sol. CREDIT: EQuS group.

It has been revealed that A set of calibration measurements for one qubit, completed autonomously by GPT‑5.6 Sol. CREDIT: EQuS group.

It has been revealed that GPT‑5.6 Sol had more difficulty when experimental signals were weak or noisy. In those cases, it took longer to find suitable measurement parameters and sometimes needed guidance from an experienced researcher. The results suggest that current agents can handle clearly defined experimental workflows, but interpreting ambiguous physical results remains a challenge.

It has been revealed that EQuS fabricates many of these standard chips, each of which can take a researcher several days to characterize. The group now regularly uses agents to handle routine measurements, freeing researchers to focus on other work.

“I can have agents running measurements for many hours overnight or while I’m working in the cleanroom,” Yankelevich said. “I can check in from my phone, see what they’ve done, and steer them if something needs fixing or if I want to explore a different direction.”.

An excerpted GPT‑5.6 Sol chain-of-thought from a calibration run. CREDIT: EQuS group.

It has been revealed that the immediate advantage is that Codex agents can help researchers make steady progress on experimental analysis and measurements without constant supervision. Experienced researchers may still be able to identify the best calibration settings faster than current AI models. But by saving time previously spent on monitoring every step of the calibration process, researchers can focus on other work.

Routine chip characterization follows a relatively well-defined workflow. For novel experiments, Yankelevich assigns Codex agents narrower experimental goals while drawing more heavily on their ability to write, modify, and test new code for control, analysis, and simulation. Connecting agents directly to the lab lets the group revise code, test it against real measurements, and complete longer stretches of work autonomously.

“I’ve built infrastructure to guide agents through several parts of my work—measurement, theory, and chip design—and now it’s really starting to pay off,” Yankelevich noted. “I can have multiple agents working on different problems at once, and I spend most of my time on higher-level work—interpreting results, devising experiments, planning next steps for the agents, reading, and writing.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, we’re announcing the appointment of Paul Christiano to the OpenAI Foundation Board.
  • Paul will also join the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the Foundation Board, working alongside its chair, Zico Kolter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paul Christiano will also join the Foundation’s Safety and Security Committee.

In a recent development, we’re announcing the appointment of Paul Christiano to the OpenAI Foundation Board. He will be a non-voting observer on the OpenAI Group PBC Board.

Paul will also join the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the Foundation Board, working alongside its chair, Zico Kolter. The SSC provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, including OpenAI Group PBC.

In a recent development, paul brings government experience spanning two administrations through his work at the Center for AI Standards and Innovation⁠(opens in a new window) (CAISI) within the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), an agency of the U.S. Department of Commerce, where he is a Senior Tech Advisor1. During his time at CAISI and its predecessor, the U.S. AI Safety Institute, Paul has worked on evaluating frontier AI models, including capabilities with national security implications, and on approaches to mitigating associated safety and security risks.

Sources indicate that paul is also the founder of the Alignment Research Center⁠(opens in a new window) (ARC), a nonprofit research organization focused on aligning advanced AI systems with human interests. From 2017 to 2021, Paul led alignment research at OpenAI and contributed foundational work on reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this new capacity, Paul brings a distinct and technically grounded perspective to OpenAI’s governance decisions. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.

Recent findings suggest that AI is entering a new era of capability, making it increasingly vital that advances in these systems are accompanied by strong safety, security, alignment and governance. Throughout Paul’s career researching AI alignment, he brings a perspective that takes seriously the possibility that advanced AI could pose catastrophic risks and that developers must prepare before systems reach more dangerous levels of capability. He has been an independent voice on whether the industry’s safeguards are adequate. We believe the Foundation’s governance is stronger with people prepared to challenge prevailing assumptions and help strengthen the evidence, safeguards, and accountability underlying critical decisions.

Industry observers note that paul’s appointment builds on the governance structure established through OpenAI’s recapitalization in October 2025, including the commitments made in connection with the reviews conducted over the course of a year by the California Attorney General⁠(opens in a new window) and Delaware Attorney General⁠(opens in a new window). Their engagement helped strengthen the governance framework.

The OpenAI Foundation is a charitable organization dedicated to ensuring AI benefits all of humanity. As a separate nonprofit organization, the Foundation conducts its own charitable operations while maintaining control of, and holding a significant equity stake in OpenAI Group PBC. The Foundation supports initiatives advancing scientific discovery, strengthening civil society, and building resilience through responsible AI. Through grants, partnerships, and other philanthropic initiatives, the Foundation helps accelerate work that creates lasting public benefit and expands access to AI’s transformative potential.

The Foundation controls OpenAI Group PBC, with the Safety and Security Committee a committee of the Foundation Board. Learn more at www.openaifoundation.org⁠(opens in a latest window).

As a Senior Technical Advisor, Paul will recuse himself from all OpenAI-related matters as well as all model evaluations.

#24943. Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (268 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (268 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.25760v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer-agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, 37.24% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains 93.06% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our most capable model, built for all the work businesses need to get done.
  • Last week we introduced GPT‑6 Astra, the world’s most intelligent and aligned model, now available in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API.
  • Industry observers note that most AI systems require businesses to prepare their data, redesign workflows, and build custom integrations before they can deliver value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our most capable model, built for all the work businesses need to get done.

Last week we introduced GPT‑6 Astra, the world’s most intelligent and aligned model, now available in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API. Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, professional work, software engineering, cybersecurity, and science, so teams can take on the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment.

Industry observers note that most AI systems require businesses to prepare their data, redesign workflows, and build custom integrations before they can deliver value. Astra changes that. In ChatGPT Work and Codex, it can write code and work through the same applications people use every day—even when those applications don’t have an API. That means businesses can put AI to work within their existing workflows from day one, without extensive preparation or engineering work.

Within the first few days of rollout, we’re already seeing customers put Astra to work, from optimizing GPUs to spotting discrepancies in financial statements to producing more on-brand decks.

Industry observers note that at OpenAI, Astra was rolled out internally weeks before launch, so we saw first hand how bleeding-edge capabilities like computer use could change the way we work. Our developer and marketing teams used Astra and Codex to turn three hours of multicamera footage into our GPT‑6 Astra Developer First Impressions video⁠(opens in a new window) which has already garnered over 550k views in just 4 days. Our engineering team used Astra to uncover and resolve a memory-allocation bottleneck that was causing slow Codex sessions in a test environment. By switching allocators, they were able to produce 25× lower turn latency with roughly 30% higher peak memory use.

Astra is also better at following a company’s voice, templates, and design standards, so the first result is closer to something a team can put to use.

According to recent reports, astra continues our commitment to providing extremely efficient models that deliver more useful work per dollar to our customers. It's been trained to complete tasks in fewer tokens with fewer retries, which means less rework and lower cost per task. With Astra, OpenAI occupies the majority of the cost-efficiency frontier on professional work and coding evaluations, including Terminal Bench 4.0 and Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Pricing starts at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens.

Industry observers note that giving AI access to business systems requires confidence in how it will act. With this in mind, Astra is our most aligned model yet, with stronger adherence to human intent and authorization.

Recent findings suggest that during training, we tested Astra on our internal computer use safety benchmark⁠ which tests models against the hardest business scenarios such as exposing confidential information, sharing a dashboard too broadly, or deleting data. In this evaluation, Astra produced unintended outcomes 89% less often than GPT‑5.6 Sol and 74.7% less often than Claude Fable 5.1. Additional confirmation and automated review further improved performance for GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑5.6 Sol.

It has been revealed that organizations can also decide how broadly to deploy Astra. New enterprise admin controls let them restrict access to approved websites and desktop applications, manage uploads and downloads, and control browsing history. ChatGPT Work and Codex also include safeguards such as confirmation policies, which can require approval before consequential actions, and automated review of potentially unsafe or unauthorized tool calls. These controls allow teams to start with a limited configuration and expand access over time.

To further access, alongside Astra, we’re also launching fresh enterprise plugins in ChatGPT Desktop. Powered by the latest browser use capabilities, plugins from Oracle Analytics, Power BI (a Microsoft Fabric service), Navan, and Avalara make it easier to access familiar enterprise applications.

Industry observers note that astra⁠(opens in a new window) is also the first model to reach the Critical cybersecurity capability threshold⁠ under our Preparedness Framework⁠. With that increased capability, we’ve strengthened protections⁠(opens in a new window) against both misuse and the model taking unauthorized actions including training Astra to respect safety and security boundaries, improving its resistance to attempts to bypass safeguards, and deploying automated checks designed to block harmful responses.

Zero Data Retention is available for eligible API customers on supported endpoints, subject to approval.

Try GPT‑6 Astra in ChatGPT Work⁠(opens in a latest window) or Codex⁠(opens in a new window), or build it into your own products and workflows through the API⁠(opens in a new window).

Enterprise administrators can enable Astra under their applicable rate card and agreement. Enterprise access is off by default at launch.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (228 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.25705v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with customers over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

arXiv:2611.25254v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current initiative. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.

arXiv:2611.25105v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

#24934. The AI policy window is open. We need to act.

📅 09 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1992 w)

AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

The AI policy window is open. We need to act.

📅 09 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Chris Lehane, Chief Global Affairs Officer at OpenAI.
  • We’ve reached a upcoming chapter in AI capabilities, and that demands a new chapter for AI policy.
  • In a recent development, pushing for mandatory national AI safety requirements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Chris Lehane, Chief Global Affairs Officer at OpenAI.

We’ve reached a upcoming chapter in AI capabilities, and that demands a new chapter for AI policy. No company, industry, or government can meet this challenge alone. We need to meet this moment with a bias toward meaningful action over policy perfection.

In a recent development, pushing for mandatory national AI safety requirements. We want to work with Congress on mandatory, capability-based national AI safety regulation.

Keeping up momentum in the states. Until Congress acts, we will continue supporting state legislation that strengthens the broader AI safety ecosystem. Today, we are announcing our support for four California bills: SB 813 on overall infrastructure for independent safety assessments, AB 1405 on AI-auditor standards, SB 1119 on protections for young people, and AB 1864 on safeguards against AI-enabled biological threats.

Advancing industry-led standards. We will work with other frontier labs to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support.

Recent findings suggest that building global standards. We will advocate for compatible international approaches to measuring capabilities, managing risk, preserving human control, and determining when and how development should slow or stop, even if that means slowing the advancement of model capabilities.

Our Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki recently wrote⁠ that the rapid rise of machine intelligence, including the potential of recursive self-improvement, calls for “extreme caution.” OpenAI will continue pursuing technical solutions to alignment and monitoring, building defensive systems, and slowing development when necessary. But technical work inside individual labs will not be enough. We also need shared standards, including regarding when development should slow or stop.

In a recent development, the stakes are enormous. Advanced AI could accelerate the development of newly introduced medicines⁠, strengthen critical infrastructure⁠, expand economic opportunity⁠, and help solve scientific problems⁠ that have resisted generations of human effort. But the capabilities that make models more useful also come with risks, and they will not remain confined to a few frontier laboratories. Models developed around the world, including open models, will increasingly approach today’s frontier and become broadly available.

Astra’s capabilities, the early evidence of AI-driven research acceleration, and Jakub’s essay all point in the same direction: AI is advancing swiftly, and policy needs to move with it.

According to recent reports, greg Brockman has described a “defenders window”⁠(opens in a newly introduced window): a limited period when frontier AI can help defenders strengthen critical systems before powerful offensive capabilities become widespread. Policymakers face an analogous moment: a closing window to establish durable safeguards before AI capabilities outpace the institutions responsible for governing them.

As capabilities grow, confidence in safety must increasingly set the pace of AI progress. Safety does not stand in the way of progress; it is what allows progress to go further and benefit more people.

According to recent reports, we have strengthened monitoring, alignment, and security safeguards across the model-development lifecycle, including stronger isolation for frontier research workloads, expanded monitoring of model behavior during tool-enabled training and evaluations, and clearer rules for when to escalate concerns. For Astra, we also introduced universal monitoring of full trajectories, including chains of thought, and a mandatory alignment-evaluation gate before broader internal deployment.

It has been revealed that those safeguards must continue to stay ahead of capabilities. When proceeding would pose an unacceptable safety risk, we will slow or stop the development or deployment of systems we cannot sufficiently safeguard, as we have done before and as required per our preparedness framework⁠(opens in a new window).

Industry observers note that fully autonomous recursive self-improvement—in which AI systems independently drive successive generations of increasingly capable AI—is not happening today. We should not pursue it unless and until it can be done safely.

Sources indicate that however, AI is already accelerating parts of the research used to develop and align the next generation of models. Our latest research⁠ demonstrates that AI agents can perform some tasks that would take skilled researchers several days. This is not recursive self-improvement, but it is evidence of the direction of travel.

Recent findings suggest that that acceleration can and must also be directed toward safety. Our aim is to safely build automated AI researchers that work under human supervision to advance both deep learning and alignment—using each generation of AI to help make the next one safer, more aligned, and easier to control, not simply more capable.

Recent findings suggest that governments should develop common ways to measure this progress, preserve meaningful human control, and establish shared safety bars for when and how development should slow or stop. If we cannot meet certain safety bars without slowing down capability growth, we should prioritize the former. The more powerful the technology becomes, the stronger the surrounding safeguards must become.

The prospect of AI-accelerated AI development demands more than voluntary commitments. The United States needs mandatory, capability-based national regulation that can evolve as the technology does.

Our Blueprint for Democratic Governance of Frontier AI⁠ lays out a path toward a durable federal framework: common testing and independent-assessment requirements, stronger cybersecurity protections, clear incident-reporting rules, greater national preparedness, and shared measures for tracking progress toward recursive self-improvement.

It has been revealed that several serious frontier safety proposals are now taking shape in Congress. We will continue to engage constructively and expect to support legislation that materially raises the safety bar. With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good. Congress should act before it adjourns.

A national framework should be strong but carefully targeted. Frontier safety requirements should apply to the handful of well-resourced laboratories developing the most capable systems—not to startups, small developers, or researchers operating nowhere near the frontier. Obligations should be proportionate to capabilities and risks.

In a recent development, nor should frontier safety policy become open-weights policy by another name. Open models can be part of the solution, particularly in cybersecurity and where sovereignty, security, or data-residency needs favor local deployment. Most compete not at the frontier, but on cost, control, and latency. As we affirmed in signing the Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter⁠(opens in a upcoming window), America needs both open and closed models. A federal framework should address frontier capabilities and risks without weakening competition, entrenching incumbents, or driving innovation overseas.

Recent findings suggest that A serious public framework should reduce, not increase, the concentration of power. Today, frontier laboratories largely set their own rules for managing frontier risks. Democratically accountable standards, independent verification, and meaningful transparency would replace that fragmented system of private governance.

This is essential to American leadership. The United States cannot win the AI era on capability alone. Being ahead technically will matter little if people, institutions, and governments do not trust the technology enough to adopt it. Strong safeguards are not a concession against innovation. They are part of the infrastructure required for widespread adoption—and for lasting American leadership.

Recent findings suggest that we badly need national standards on AI, and anyone working at the frontier can see the urgency. Until Congress acts, states should continue to move to fill the vacuum and raise the bar.

Sources indicate that openAI has supported California’s SB 53, New York’s RAISE Act, Illinois’s SB 315, and independent audits in the frontier safety legislation under consideration in Massachusetts. We encourage states to converge around these common safeguards. As they do, they can create a de facto national baseline that Congress can ultimately codify—an approach we call ⁠reverse federalism⁠. But harmonization does not mean freezing requirements in place.

Today, we are formally endorsing four additional California bills that have passed the legislature and are headed to Governor Newsom. Together, they address complementary parts of the AI-safety ecosystem.

In a recent development, SB 813⁠(opens in a fresh window) would establish a process for designating qualified, independent organizations capable of assessing AI risks. As we have stated in our ⁠(opens in a new window)frontier safety blueprint⁠(opens in a new window), we prefer independent technical assessments to be required at the federal level, where policymakers can establish consistent standards for assessor qualifications, security, and access to highly sensitive information. In the absence of federal action, however, California can help establish the rules of the road for a secure, capable national independent-assessment system that produces better safety outcomes.

AB 1405⁠(opens in a latest window) would create registration, independence, transparency, and accountability requirements for AI auditors.

According to recent reports, SB 1119⁠(opens in a fresh window) would require age assurance, risk assessments, independent audits, parental controls, and safeguards against harmful content for children and teens using companion chatbots. We recently signaled our support⁠ of this bill, which builds on youth-safety measures OpenAI has advanced through our products, ⁠global policy principles⁠, and support for the ⁠(opens in a new window)Parents & Kids Safe AI Act⁠(opens in a new window), as well as protections built into ChatGPT for Teens—including stronger defaults in sensitive areas, Quiet Hours, Study Hours, and break reminders.

AB 1864⁠(opens in a latest window) would require gene-synthesis providers and manufacturers of benchtop synthesis equipment to follow federal screening standards, strengthening an notable physical safeguard against AI-enabled biological threats.

Some of these bills we did not endorse in the past, and are now supporting after reconsidering in light of the recent jump in capabilities we have seen.

These bills are not a substitute for federal regulation. They are serious efforts that can protect people now, demonstrate what workable safeguards look like, and help build momentum for federal action.

Industry observers note that laws alone will not make advanced AI safe. We also need concrete practices inside the laboratories developing the most capable systems. The most urgent place to start is monitoring.

According to recent reports, this is particularly important for misalignment—when a model pursues an objective in ways that violate human intent or established boundaries, without requiring consciousness or malicious intent. As models gain greater autonomy, use more powerful tools, and operate over longer periods, developers should be required to monitor for these misaligned behaviors and demonstrate that effective safeguards are in place.

It has been revealed that monitoring must be connected to clear disclosure requirements. As we advocated in California, companies should be required to provide prompt written notice to affected parties when, during development or evaluation, their models circumvent another organization’s security controls without authorization and materially access, alter, or destroy that organization’s protected systems or confidential information. We also support federal reporting requirements for other serious AI incidents and are working to define which incidents should be covered and what those requirements should entail.

As we shared last week, OpenAI is developing a framework for reporting consequential misalignment incidents and systematically monitoring frontier-model activity, including internal use. This is beginning as a company-led effort, but we hope it can help inform broader federal policy and reporting requirements.

We want to work with other labs on industry-led standards. Any industry-led standards would complement—not replace—mandatory federal safeguards and democratic oversight. But we have entered a different phase of AI capabilities, and everything should be on the table—including considering what can be built voluntarily outside government as an immediate step.

Any such standards must ultimately also extend beyond national borders. Models, research, and technical expertise move globally, and failures involving the most capable systems could have consequences far beyond the country in which they are developed. The United States needs to establish credible standards at home if it is going to lead internationally—and we are increasingly convinced that compatible international standards will be necessary.

According to recent reports, the AI policy window is open, for now. We intend to use it.

That means acting with urgency, humility, and a willingness to adapt. It means supporting serious proposals that materially raise the safety bar, even when they are not exactly what we would have designed. And it means strengthening the framework as the technology evolves.

No first step will be perfect. But the greater risk now is waiting too long to take one.

arXiv:2611.25086v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide latest living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.

Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

  • We’re launching GPT‑Live‑1 in the API, giving developers a powerful, natural voice model for building voice-enabled apps and business workflows.
  • For the API release of GPT‑Live‑1, we’ve focused on new capabilities that let developers steer and customize voice experiences around their owners, workflows, and goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GPT‑Live‑1 brings ChatGPT’s natural, full-duplex conversations to the API, with more control over how voice agents speak and act.

We’re launching GPT‑Live‑1 in the API, giving developers a powerful, natural voice model for building voice-enabled apps and business workflows. First introduced in ChatGPT, GPT‑Live‑1 is capable of listening and speaking at the same time, and, as seen with Codex and ChatGPT Work⁠(opens in a latest window), can delegate deeper reasoning and actions to the models and tools it is paired with.

For the API release of GPT‑Live‑1, we’ve focused on new capabilities that let developers steer and customize voice experiences around their owners, workflows, and goals. A core GPT‑Live‑1 strength, smooth interruption handling, is already delivering business impact: in early evaluations, Speak found that GPT‑Live‑1 gave learners more time to think before the language tutor responded, cutting interruptions by almost 80% versus previous turn-based systems.

Key strengths of GPT‑Live‑1 in the API:.

Interruption handling: Improves interruption handling via a single model that reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together, avoiding the latency and brittle handoffs of chained STT–LLM–TTS architectures.

Reasoning & tool calling delegation: GPT‑Live‑1 can delegate reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model like GPT‑6 Astra or a third-party model.

Tone, pace, and style: Lets developers shape an agent’s tone, pace, and conversational style through the system prompt.

Silent context management & background noise: Better handles background noise and silence without interrupting the conversation or narrating every step out loud.

Long-session reliability: Improves context retention and conversational quality across extended interactions.

Telephony support: Enables deployment of full-duplex voice agents for phone calls, from restaurant reservations to customer support.

Traditional voice agents stitch together speech-to-text, a reasoning model, and text-to-speech. Each handoff adds latency and creates more opportunities to lose timing, context, or the natural rhythm of a conversation. Developers are often the ones left coordinating those stages, including what happens when someone interrupts, pauses, or changes direction.

Industry observers note that GPT‑Live‑1 handles listening and speaking in a single model, simplifying the voice layer. It can respond to interruptions and acknowledgements as they happen, while delegating deeper reasoning to the back end. This lets the conversation continue while work happens in the background.

It has been revealed that developers choose the models, tools, and agent harness behind the conversation. For example, they might pair GPT‑Live‑1 with a model like Luna for high-volume tasks like scheduling or order updates, and use a model like Astra for complex customer issues that require reasoning. That flexibility lets developers match reasoning depth, speed, and cost to each task.

Recent findings suggest that GPT‑Live‑1 natively provides ASR transcripts and response text. It also offers strong alphanumeric understanding and supports keyword biasing. Although GPT‑Live‑1 is not a turn-based model, it natively supports turn detection, so developers can continue to build around explicit turn boundaries.

Across our evaluations, GPT‑Live‑1 improves Full Duplex Bench performance by 30 percentage points over GPT‑Realtime‑2.1, with large gains in turn-taking latency and interactive behavior. Paired with GPT‑6 Astra at medium reasoning effort, it also ranks #1 on Tau3, which measures frontier voice-agent intelligence on end-to-end tasks.

It has been revealed that evaluates spoken customer-service tasks in airline, retail, and telecom domains. Pass@1 measures task success; the headline gives each domain equal weight.

* GPT Live backend: Astra (medium).

Sources indicate that evaluates spoken banking support with knowledge retrieval and account tools. Pass@1 is the fraction of 97 banking_knowledge tasks completed successfully.

* GPT Live backend: Astra (medium).

Evaluates pause handling, conversational turn taking, interruptions, and backchannels.

Tests reactions to background speech, speech to another person, listener backchannels, and interruptions.

Measures how swiftly the agent starts its reply after the user finishes a turn.

Industry observers note that tests tool use from spoken requests containing natural pauses, hesitations, and self-corrections. Pass@1 scores the tool-call sequence.

* GPT Live backend: Terra (low).

Evaluates the spoken answer to tool-using requests containing pauses, hesitations, and self-corrections. Scores how well the answer matches the reference intent.

* GPT Live backend: Terra (low).

Industry observers note that developers need voices that fit their product and sound natural to the people using it. With GPT‑Live‑1, we’re expanding from a small set of real-time voices to a broader selection across accents, dialects, and languages giving developers more choice in how their assistants sound.

We’ll continue to expand voice options and language availability over the coming months.

Sources indicate that GPT‑Live‑1 is available in the API today⁠(opens in a new window) at $0.05 per minute for the front-end voice layer. Pair it with the backend model and agent harness that fit your product, then build a voice experience that can scale with the work it needs to do.

Latest Update: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (213 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.23353v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (347 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22537v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion proposal, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new aims 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.

Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (179 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21880v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $\delta$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/\delta)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Build and run cloud agents with the Codex harness, fully managed by OpenAI.
  • As we’ve scaled Codex and ChatGPT for Work to millions of people around the world, we’ve learned what it takes to make long-running agents work well in practice.
  • Today, we’re introducing the Agents API⁠(opens in a latest window) in public beta, bringing that same harness and infrastructure that powers Codex to developers through a simple, flexible API.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Build and run cloud agents with the Codex harness, fully managed by OpenAI.

As we’ve scaled Codex and ChatGPT for Work to millions of people around the world, we’ve learned what it takes to make long-running agents work well in practice. Useful agents need a powerful harness that manages context, uses tools efficiently, and coordinates subagents. They also need infrastructure that keeps them running reliably for days, with environments where they can work with files, run code, and save intermediate results.

Today, we’re introducing the Agents API⁠(opens in a latest window) in public beta, bringing that same harness and infrastructure that powers Codex to developers through a simple, flexible API.

With the Agents API, you can create a production-ready agent in a single API call by specifying the task, model, tools, and environment:.

Recent findings suggest that openAI hosts and maintains the harness. You choose the agent’s compute environment: in an OpenAI-managed sandbox, on your own infrastructure, or with one of our sandbox partners. The Agents API gives you a strong foundation for building agents on top of our optimized agent harness and infrastructure, so you can focus on the tools, knowledge, and workflows that make your agent unique.

Agents API powers your agents with the same harness and infrastructure behind Codex.

Different workloads need different compute, storage, and deployment options. The Agents API lets you choose a sandbox that fits your application.

We’re partnering with ecosystem providers⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), including Blaxel, Cloudflare, Daytona, DigitalOcean, E2B, Modal, Oracle, Runloop, and Vercel, to provide first-class integrations for a range of needs:.

Fully managed environments or deployments within your VPC.

Specific file and secret storage mechanisms.

Different CPU, GPU, and memory configurations, with performance, cold-start, and cost profiles to match your tech giant’s workflow.

The Agents API offers first-class integrations with popular ecosystem providers.

For developers who want to get started promptly and scale efficiently, we’re also introducing the OpenAI hosted sandbox⁠(opens in a newly introduced window). This leverages the same sandboxing infrastructure that powers Codex and ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, openAI provisions and manages the sandbox, giving your agent a secure and performant environment to run code, work with files, and produce artifacts. These sandboxes can be flexibly configured with your files, packages, skills and plugins to give the agent what it needs to complete the task.

Industry observers note that taking advantage of new model capabilities often means reworking your harness, taking valuable time away from improving your application. The Agents API provides versioned access to these capabilities with each model launch. We maintain and continuously improve the harness alongside our models, helping your agents get better performance from every upgrade. For example, recent improvements to the harness include:.

According to recent reports, to support models working for hours, we’ve built context management that helps agents carry relevant information across longer sessions. The Agents API automatically compacts⁠(opens in a new window) earlier context as a session approaches its context limit, preserving information the agent needs to continue. Developers can build workflows that span multiple context windows without implementing their own compaction logic.

The Agents API helps agents find the right tools and use them efficiently. Tool search⁠(opens in a new window) loads relevant tool definitions as needed, helping reduce token usage and cost while preserving the model’s cache. Once tools are available, programmatic tool calling⁠(opens in a new window) lets agents run calls in parallel, chain related operations, and filter or combine results in code so they can work through large volumes of data while bringing only the relevant results back into context. The Agents API supports MCP, custom functions, and built-in tools like web search.

Sources indicate that with multi-agent support⁠(opens in a new window), the Agents API can break complex tasks into independent pieces and delegate them to subagents that work in parallel. Each subagent maintains its own context, helping it stay focused on its assignment, while the main agent coordinates their work and brings the results together. This can speed up research, analysis, and coding tasks that benefit from parallel work, without requiring you to build your own orchestration.

The Agents API is powered by the open-source Codex harness, giving developers visibility into the core logic that coordinates model calls, tools, and context. With the Agents API, OpenAI operates and maintains that harness while developers can inspect and learn from its public codebase⁠(opens in a fresh window).

Agents API is available in public beta today to all developers. There are no additional fees for using the Agents API – you simply pay for the tokens and tools your agents use, as outlined on our pricing page⁠(opens in a new window).

Explore the Agents API overview⁠(opens in a fresh window) to learn more, or follow the quickstart⁠(opens in a new window) to get started and bring the harness behind Codex into your own agents.

During the public beta, we’ll iterate quickly based on your feedback as we work toward general availability. Let us know what’s working, where you’re running into friction, and what you need to build and run your agents in production.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.21797v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (268 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.19151v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Marine and offshore engineering knowledge is scattered across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, but remains small by pretraining standards. We examine how far parameter-efficient adaptation can take a lightweight domain model on a workstation-class device. Starting from OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we trained two LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training on one NVIDIA DGX Spark took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second. The first used next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. Of 13,879 source documents, 7,069 remained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter to remove cross-domain lexical collisions. Validation loss fell from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. After the continuation adapter drifted off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, we trained an instruction adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs: 114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages. Loss was applied only to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts, hand-scored for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the base model, continuation adapter, instruction adapter and instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 81. The retrieval score reflects a corrected index-leakage concern. A paired test supports the instruction-tuning gain but finds no retrieval benefit on this set. Accuracy remained low: 14/40 without retrieval and 16/40 with it. A second evaluation used prompts from passages excluded from both instruction-data splits, addressing selection leakage in round one. It confirmed the instruction-tuning gain (p=0.0001 and p=0.0002) and found that retrieval significantly helped the base model, but not the instruction adapter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A first-of-its-kind agreement will provide free access and 50% off usage for federal, state, local, and tribal governments, alongside expanded support and access for public-sector cyber defenders.
  • Sources indicate that america’s public servants, including those on the front lines of cyber defense, should have access to the best AI tools available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first-of-its-kind agreement will provide free access and 50% off usage for federal, state, local, and tribal governments, alongside expanded support and access for public-sector cyber defenders.

Sources indicate that america’s public servants, including those on the front lines of cyber defense, should have access to the best AI tools available. Today, OpenAI for Government and the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) are announcing a new multi-year agreement that builds on last year’s federal offer. This first-of-its-kind agreement will provide $0 access—normally $15 per user per month—for the license fee and 50% off usage, alongside expanded support for public-sector cyber defenders. OpenAI is also extending the same offer to all state, local and tribal governments.

Helping government work better—making services faster, easier, safer, and more reliable—is a key way to bring the benefits of AI to everyone. Public servants should help shape how AI is used in government, and that starts by giving them access to best-in-class tools, including GPT‑6 Astra, with strong safeguards, cost predictability and respect for their public mission. More than one million government employees already have access to ChatGPT through our existing agreements, and this expanded partnership extends eligibility across a U.S. public-sector workforce of approximately 23 million people.

Over the past year, public servants have shown what broader access to OpenAI tools can make possible:.

Daybreak Access is improving the speed and quality of vulnerability research, malware analysis, and security-tool development for government cyber defenders.

The CDC accelerated public-health literature reviews that previously took days or months, producing most initial reports in under 30 minutes, with productivity gains reported by 92% of participating experts.

Georgia’s Department of Revenue reduced the time needed to digitize a tax form from as much as two weeks to 15 minutes.

In North Carolina, the Department of State Treasurer used ChatGPT to identify millions of dollars in potential unclaimed property that could be returned to residents.

Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory used ChatGPT to accelerate development of a preliminary fusion-research model, compressing work that could have taken months into a matter of hours.

Industry observers note that with this announcement, we are also expanding support for government cyber defenders protecting emergency response, transportation, public health, utilities, and other critical systems. Secure and responsible deployment: ChatGPT Enterprise does not use business data, including inputs or outputs, to train or improve OpenAI models, and participating organizations will retain the protections associated with the eligible services they choose.

SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (234 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.19050v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement over 72 Valid Experimental Cells

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (224 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.13223v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reasoning models write a trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read it. Upstream providers hold different retention constraints, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and its task cost remains unmeasured. This paper reports a direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, a calibrated set of 72 valid experimental cells, a multi-seed protocol, and the official checker. The same deletion separates the models by direction and by magnitude, one class losing tens of points, another gaining, and a third unchanged, with the endpoint ordering reproduced across seeds and task subsets modulating the magnitude and, near zero, the sign. A re-dosed model preserves its success across the full deletion range, so the reading belongs to the model rather than the dose. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property under an operational definition, measured under a fixed task family, scorer, and protocol, and a retrained model is a latest model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.

Frontier intelligence, built for financial services.

We’re introducing ChatGPT for Financial Services, a tailored ChatGPT Work experience that combines built-in financial data with GPT‑6 Astra⁠’s reasoning to help teams develop research, financial models, and customized client materials.

Industry observers note that this product has been shaped by our design partnership with Morgan Stanley and Evercore. The collaboration has enabled us to pinpoint where OpenAI can solve the biggest challenges for financial institutions and has guided us on the solutions that will help every banker in their day-to-day work.

Recent findings suggest that built-in premium data from providers like Daloopa, PitchBook, LSEG News, and Crunchbase remove the challenges with MCP connectors and access to data. This data is indexed and hosted by OpenAI to enable higher accuracy and fresh features like granular citations so that bankers can trace figures and claims back to their sources, and check the evidence as their analysis develops.

In a recent development, the product also offers state of the art frontier intelligence, including GPT‑6 Astra, natively and will continue to have newer models available out of the box as they are released. Firms can also centrally manage access and data connections, supported by ChatGPT’s enterprise security and governance controls.

According to recent reports, our early work with Morgan Stanley and Evercore has helped steer where we have started: investment banking and equity research. Reliable access to data and high quality artifact creation proved to be the biggest pain points for their teams. Our work with partners will inform post training, product improvements, and our expansion into other financial services categories.

It has been revealed that chatGPT for Financial Services brings together the financial data teams need, with the depth of detail expected. We’ve included premium financial data, streamlined existing provider connections, and improved MCP performance.

ChatGPT for Financial Services brings together built-in data, connected sources, and financial analysis workflows.

ChatGPT for Financial Services includes datasets from providers like Daloopa, PitchBook, LSEG News and Crunchbase covering earnings transcripts, financial statements, tech giant fundamentals, private companies, and more.

Teams can start working with these datasets immediately, with no separate contracts to negotiate or connectors to set up. We index and host this data on OpenAI infrastructure, allowing us to improve retrieval, latency, and how we surface it in the product experience.

For a banker running a P&L normalization analysis, that means being able to inspect the reconciliation and notes behind an adjusted EBITDA, understanding which costs were excluded, and deciding how to use it in a valuation.

Our partners are central to this work and as we expand coverage, we will continue to deepen our models’ understanding of these datasets. We will post train our models to find, interpret, and use this data like we know the best analysts can.

Trace figures and claims to specific tables and passages, with the supporting information highlighted for review.

It has been revealed that we know many customers already have existing data subscriptions. So we’re working with S&P Capital IQ, LSEG, MSCI, Dow Jones Factiva, and Moody’s on shared sign-in and entitlement integrations. Providers will be able to recognize users through their ChatGPT sign-in to enable automatic access to data they’re already entitled to.

Sources indicate that it can be challenging to effectively use MCP connectors for data providers. We have focused on making some of the most used MCPs in financial services optimized for immediate use in the product, so teams can spend less time troubleshooting requests and more time on analysis.

Our broader connector ecosystem includes over 50+ connectors including Datasite, Box, Preqin, FactSet and Intapp.

GPT‑6 Astra is state of the art across three of the core capabilities required for financial services work: information retrieval, financial reasoning, and artifact generation.

It can navigate and understand figures, tables, and the supporting notes in financial documents. It can take inputs, run financial analysis, and draw conclusions. And it can take all of this work and accurately synthesize it into documents, spreadsheets, and slides.

We’ve built fundamental capabilities into the product so that it can research across multiple sources, trace figures across different periods, and interpret annotations in public data. Once that analysis is complete, teams can build interactive charts and visualizations.

Compare company performance in interactive charts, with the underlying data and sources available for review.

In ChatGPT for Financial Services, administrators can publish Excel, Word, and PowerPoint templates through a dedicated admin page. With firm templates and style guides configured, teams can turn their analysis into valuation models, research notes, and pitchbooks in their firm’s format and style.

Publish firm templates to the teams who use them.

Industry observers note that your firm’s business data is not used to train our models by default. It is encrypted at rest and in transit, and admins can configure workspace retention. Compliance teams can export supported workspace logs through the OpenAI Compliance Platform into their existing audit and investigation workflows.

Industry observers note that firms can manage access to skills and apps by role and enable or disable supported app read and write actions. Multiple workspaces can also be created to enforce information barriers.

Industry observers note that chatGPT for Financial Services is one way we serve customers across the industry, but we recognize that it will require a range of solutions to address the needs of the finance industry. OpenAI has a long history of collaborating with innovators to unlock novel AI solutions. Financial services firms and developers can use our API to build specialized applications for the needs they understand best. OpenAI brings frontier models and the capabilities to put them to work. Financial institutions, data providers, and software partners bring specialized expertise, trusted information, and customer relationships.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.12508v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalizing deepfake detection across facial manipulation and fully generated video remains challenging due to forgery traces varying with the manipulation method and scene content. Explicit spatial and temporal feature differences offer a way to capture this variation, but also respond to natural texture and motion, motivating their joint interpretation with appearance features. We investigate whether combining multiscale feature differences with adapted appearance representations improves detection across both forgery categories. We introduce Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams (MARS), a two-path video detector. The residual path applies fixed spatial and temporal difference-of-Gaussians operators to frozen intermediate features and models the resulting differences alongside appearance context across frames. The semantic path adapts the encoder's normalization parameters for frame classification, and a clip-dependent gate combines their predictions. Under a shared protocol across seven datasets, MARS achieves the highest average AUROC of 91.43\%, outperforming seven compared detectors. When trained on facial manipulations alone, MARS achieves 93.99\% AUROC on GenVideo and 75.50\% on DF26, demonstrating transfer to generated videos without generated-video training data. MARS also provides signed patch and frame contributions, whose faithfulness we evaluate through controlled spatial and temporal removal against random controls. MARS is publicly available for research: Project page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mars/ Github: https://github.com/VectorInstitute/mars.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (268 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.12180v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (226 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.07695v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
